name: Debris hut
summary: A one-person A-frame packed with a metre of leaf litter — a shelter that keeps you alive overnight with no tools and no fire.

steps.text: Pick high, dry ground away from dead standing trees, drainage lines and the base of slopes where cold air pools.
Prop one end of the ridgepole at chest height on a stump or fork; the other end rests on the ground.
Lean ribbing sticks along both sides at a steep angle, close enough that leaves will not fall through. Keep the interior JUST big enough to lie in.
steps.why: The shelter is heated by your body alone. Every extra litre of interior is volume you have to warm all night.

steps.text: Pile leaf litter over the whole frame to a depth of at least an arm's length — deeper than feels sensible. Compress it and add more.
Stuff the inside with dry litter until you have to burrow in. That bedding is what insulates you from the ground, which steals more heat than the air does.
Plug the entrance behind you with a bundle of debris.

verify: Inside, in daylight, you should see no pinholes of light through the roof — a hole that passes light passes rain.
You should have to WORM into it. If you can sit up comfortably, it is too big to stay warm.
limits: It is a heat trap, not a heat source. In deep cold it extends your survival time; it does not make the night comfortable.
It takes hours of daylight and a lot of energy. Started at dusk, it is worse than an existing hollow or a tarp.
It sheds rain poorly compared to any real waterproof layer.
cautions: Never build under a dead tree or a hanging limb.
No fire inside or at the mouth — dry leaf litter is exactly the wrong material to have around a flame.
Ground contact is the main heat loss. A great roof over bare earth will still leave you hypothermic.
